The nacelle design and optimization process was split into two independent optimization steps: intake and fan cowl optimization, and bypass duct and nozzle optimization.
The intake and exhaust boundary conditions were decoupled to investigate the performance of the intake and exhaust systems independently.
The optimization algorithm used was based on an adaptive response surface methodology, which employs Kriging approximation to generate the surrogate model.
The final optimized nacelle design had a cruise drag of 26.9 drag counts.
The optimized bypass nozzle achieved a maximum velocity coefficient (Cv) of 0.9914 at a corresponding discharge coefficient (Cd) of 0.995.
The grid independence study showed that a mesh with 4.41 x 10^5 elements was sufficient to achieve grid convergence.
The loop 2 optimized design showed fully attached flow under 30 knots crosswind conditions, while the loop 1 design experienced heavy separation.
The key design parameters for the intake and fan cowl optimization were the throat radius, contraction ratio, aspect ratio, intake length, leading edge radius, and position of maximum diameter.
The axisymmetric design approach resulted in a trade-off between good cruise performance and off-design (crosswind) performance.
The iCST approach was used to parameterize the intake, fan cowl, bypass duct, and bypass nozzle geometries.
The optimization was performed separately for the intake-cowl and exhaust system, assuming minimal aerodynamic interactions between the two.
The objective for the intake-fan cowl optimization was to minimize cruise drag, while for the bypass nozzle it was to maximize the net thrust of the engine stream tube.
The Spalart-Allmaras (SA) turbulence model was used for the cruise condition simulations, while the K-omega SST model was used for the crosswind simulations.
The response surface was able to predict the cruise drag to an accuracy of 6%.
The optimized bypass nozzle design resulted in a 3.4% improvement in net propulsive force compared to the baseline.
